title: Ibrance (palbociclib): Safety and Risk Management
summary: Ibrance (palbociclib) is an oral CDK4/6 inhibitor approved by FDA (initial approval 2015) for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer, used in combination with an aromatase inhibitor, fulvestrant, or (more recently) inavolisib plus fulvestrant. Its safety profile is dominated by hematologic toxicity—principally neutropenia, which is the most common adverse reaction across pivotal trials—along with infections, fatigue, GI effects, and rarer but serious risks of interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis, embryo-fetal toxicity, and venous thromboembolism. Management relies on routine complete blood count (CBC) monitoring, defined dose-interruption/reduction algorithms for hematologic and non-hematologic toxicity, and prompt discontinuation for severe ILD/pneumonitis. Ibrance does not carry an FDA boxed warning or a REMS program based on the labeling and FDA materials reviewed; adverse events should be reported to FDA MedWatch and/or Pfizer.

claims.text: IBRANCE (palbociclib) is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with hormone receptor (HR)-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer in combination with an aromatase inhibitor, fulvestrant, or inavolisib plus fulvestrant (the latter for endocrine-resistant, PIK3CA-mutated disease following recurrence on or after adjuvant endocrine therapy).

claims.text: IBRANCE can cause fetal harm (embryo-fetal toxicity); patients should be advised of potential risk to a fetus and use effective contraception. Advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 3 weeks after the last dose, and advise male patients with female partners of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose.

claims.text: Safety and effectiveness of IBRANCE in pediatric patients have not been established/studied; in exploratory pediatric trials (98 patients 2 to <17 years given IBRANCE with chemotherapy, and 42 patients 4 to <17 years given IBRANCE as a single agent for recurrent/refractory solid tumors or CNS tumors), no new safety signals were observed and pediatric exposures were within the adult range for a similar body-surface-area-based dose.

claims.text: IBRANCE tablets should be swallowed whole and not chewed, crushed, or split, and no tablet should be taken if broken, cracked, or otherwise not intact; if a dose is vomited or missed, an additional dose should not be taken and the next prescribed dose should be taken at the usual time. IBRANCE tablets may be taken with or without food, whereas the capsule formulation must be taken with food.

gaps: Search results reviewed did not include an explicit statement confirming whether IBRANCE currently has or lacks an FDA REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) program; no REMS materials were located in the sources reviewed, and this should be independently verified against the current FDA REMS database before asserting its absence with certainty.

Detailed current dose-reduction schedule (e.g., specific mg levels for first/second dose reduction from 125 mg to 100 mg to 75 mg) was referenced in FDA label tables but the full table content/text was not fully captured in search snippets; the complete Table 2/Table 3 dose-modification schedules (hematologic and non-hematologic toxicities, including liver/renal impairment adjustments) should be reviewed directly in the full prescribing information PDF for complete detail.

No specific quantitative data were found in the reviewed sources on ILD/pneumonitis incidence broken down by combination partner (e.g., inavolisib combination) beyond capsule/tablet label references; PATINA-specific ILD rates were noted but detailed comparative analysis across all combination regimens was not fully available in search results.

FAERS-based real-world pharmacovigilance signal analyses (e.g., disproportionality/reporting odds ratio studies for ILD) were identified in the literature (e.g., JADER/FAERS study) but full quantitative results were not extracted in this search; interested readers should consult the primary study directly for effect estimates.

Renal and hepatic impairment-specific dose modification details were referenced in label sections but not fully captured in retrieved snippets and should be verified directly against the current full prescribing information.
warnings: Adverse event frequency percentages cited (e.g., neutropenia 80%/83%, ILD/pneumonitis 1%) are derived from specific pivotal trials (PALOMA-1/2/3, PATINA) with defined patient populations and combination partners (letrozole, fulvestrant, trastuzumab ± pertuzumab); these rates should not be extrapolated across different combination regimens, patient populations (e.g., pediatric, male patients with limited data), or treatment settings without caution, per the instruction to avoid estimating event rates across incompatible populations.

Some content was sourced from Pfizer-affiliated promotional/medical information webpages (pfizermedical.com, pfizerpro.com, pfizermedicalinformation.com) rather than directly from the FDA-hosted label PDF or DailyMed in all instances; where possible, cross-referencing was done against DailyMed and FDA.report label mirrors and the FDA-hosted PDF label, but the FDA-hosted full PDF text was only partially retrievable via search snippets, so some granular label table content (exact dose reduction levels in mg) was not independently confirmed from the primary FDA PDF text in this research pass.

Postmarketing adverse reaction data (e.g., venous thromboembolism, additional ILD/pneumonitis fatalities) are drawn from voluntary reporting systems where causality and true incidence cannot be reliably established, per the label's own caveat.

This section reflects information available as of the search date and drug label versions retrieved; because IBRANCE labeling has been updated multiple times (including for new combination indications such as inavolisib/fulvestrant), users should confirm they are referencing the most current FDA-approved label version for clinical decision-making.
